newsitem.title: UK: Fannie Mae sets first stg global bond.
newsitem.headline: Fannie Mae sets first stg global bond.

text.p: U.S. home loans group Fannie Mae broke new ground on Wednesday as it priced the first-ever sterling global bond, and the agency said it was looking at issuing in French francs as well.

"Clearly with the international focus on sterling over the past year and the attraction of the market, there was a requirement for a large liquid global issue," said a syndicate manager for BZW, joint lead manager of the bond.
The sterling syndicate manager at Merrill Lynch, the other joint lead, said investors bought the deal for its liquidity and benchmark status.
Sterling has been one of the strongest key currencies around in recent months and bankers said people had been working for some time on the concept of a sterling global issue.
Global bonds are issued simultaneously in Asia, Europe and the U.S. and Fannie Mae has launched mark and yen-denominated global bonds in the past.

Fannie Mae treasurer Linda Knight told Reuters a French franc global bond was also still a possibility. But so far it had not been economical to issue one, she said, noting inopportune conditions in the swaps market.
Knight said there was strong interest in the sterling global from British money managers, banks and building societies as it was the first time an entity was able to launch such a deal.
"Sterling worked as both the original market and the swap market were there for us," she said.
Both lead managers said the Bank of England approved the sterling bond and had been entirely supportive of it.

The 1.0 billion stg June 2002 bond was priced to yield 10 basis points over the 7.0 percent British government bond (gilt) due June 2002. The spread tightened to trade at 8.5 basis points when the deal was freed to trade.

"The driving force behind the success of the deal was Fannie Mae's triple-A credit quality, its strong financial condition and the good base of knowledge investors had of its paper," Knight said, adding the proceeds of the transaction would be swapped into dollars.
Fannie Mae is rated triple-A by both Moody's Investors Service and Standard & Poor's.
Traders have said sterling benefits from its status as a "safe haven" currency, unlikely to join European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) at the outset.
Also, Britain currently boasts one of the strongest growth rates among major economic powers and interest rates are expected to rise over coming months.
Sterling has appreciated by 15 percent against its trading partners on a trade-weighted basis since August.
Fannie Mae added that the ramifications of EMU were not the main force behind the choice of sterling.
"We are quite aware of EMU and the countries that may or may not be in or out, but it was really an economically driven transaction," Knight said.
The total order book between the two joint lead managers was 1.65 billion stg, BZW's syndicate manager said.
"The quality of the orders was of the highest rank and we had a tight quality control," he said.
He said 47 percent of the paper sold into Britain, 20 percent sold to Asian accounts, 18 percent into Continental Europe and 15 percent into the U.S.
